..
Issued at 251 PM EDT Mon Aug 3 2026

Currently-Tonight...Early convection on the west coast has once 
again blanketed much of the peninsula in mid to upper level 
clouds, limiting potential for destabilization from daytime 
heating. The only areas that managed to see decent sunlight were 
south of I-4, and outflow from the earlier convection offset that 
destabilization some. While scattered to numerous showers with 
embedded isolated lightning storms remain possible thanks to the 
high moisture and broad upper level support from the nearby 
trough, the prospect for stronger storms seems to now be limited 
to the coast from the Cape south, and even that is being upset by 
the outflow overrunning the sea breeze before the boundary can 
develop much. Storms here will be capable of gusty winds to 55 
mph, frequent lightning, and torrential downpours. While 
convection elsewhere is expected to be weaker, the enhanced 20-25 
kt steering flow means even moderate convection could produce 
gusts to 45 mph. The potential for rainfall amounts over 2" has 
decreased due to how convection evolved, but there still remains a
threat for locally high rainfall amounts that could lead to minor
flooding of low-lying areas, especially along the coast south of 
the Cape. Afternoon highs near to slightly below normal in the 
U80s-L90s thanks to the high cloud cover. Rain chances drop in the
evening but once again don't go away in the overnight, and a 
20-30% is maintained.

Tuesday...A lobe of upper-level energy becomes cut-off over the 
Deep South at the parent trough that has been resident over the 
eastern US that last few days lifts away. The elongated surface 
low centered over the Northeast ejects with the trough, but the 
abandoned mid-level disturbance to the south will help keep the 
trailing front draped across the the North Gulf states in place. 
Offshore flow will continue a bit longer between the front and 
high pressure over the western Atlantic, but will weaken and 
become more southerly. High moisture in the weakening offshore 
flow remains over the area, but not as anomalously high as 
previous days, supporting 40-60% rain chances in the afternoon and
evening, and should finally see an end to the overnight rain 
chances. Could even see rain chances drop across the northern 
counties if the mid-level low manages to develop a weak surface 
low and advect drier air towards North Florida. There is again 
potential for early convection near the west coast to upset how 
things evolve the rest of the day, so confidence in exact timing 
and strength is very low. Scattered to numerous showers with 
isolated embedded storms are expected in areas clouded over, while
locations that get sunlight could see higher coverage heavier 
showers and stronger lightning storms. 

Wednesday-Thursday...High pressure over the western Atlantic and 
its surface projection shift closer to the Eastern Seaboard as the
cut-off low is lifted into a broad trough swinging down to the to
the northern Plains and Ohio valley. Winds start light and 
variable Wednesday morning, then become onshore (easterly) in the 
afternoon, where they'll remain through the rest of the week. The 
onshore flow will allow the east coast sea breeze to push well 
inland, shifting the highest rain chances over the interior. The 
plume of high moisture will linger over the area Wednesday, before
being ushered west, with closer to normal moisture advecting 
across the peninsula Thursday. Better daytime heating looks to 
offset the lost moisture, and rain chances remain 40-60%. Could 
see an early start to showers and storms near and along the east 
coast, then moving inland with a collision over the interior 
Wednesday, and closer to the west coast Thursday.

Friday-Sunday...The synoptic pattern remains largely unchanged.
High pressure over the western Atlantic is flattened and shunted
some as the trough to our north pushes towards the Mid-Atlantic
seaboard and offshore, but the surface high will stay nearly
stationary off the southeast seaboard, keeping the ridge axis to
the north and us in onshore flow. Models continue to bring a weak
disturbance and higher moisture towards Florida along the southern
edge of the Bermuda high. Latest trends have generally been
weaker, most bringing an open wave that half of which recurve
offshore causing little to no local impact, and the other half
recurve over/near Florida but vary how far north/south. A few
solutions develop more of a trough, which further complicates the
forecast by introducing advection of drier air on the
western/southern side of the feature. Therefore, it is too early
to tell what if any impacts this wave could bring, but the return
of high rain chances and minor flooding impacts are on the table.
Otherwise, near typical Florida summer conditions with afternoon
thunderstorms and highs in the U80s-L90s, possibly creeping
towards the M90s inland.
